title: DBT definition and purpose
content: DBT is a structured psychotherapy that combines acceptance-oriented strategies with efforts to change behaviours and improve functioning. It was originally developed for people with chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder and has since been adapted for other problems.

title: Dialectical balance: acceptance and change
content: DBT balances accepting a person as they are in the present moment with efforts to change behaviours and improve functioning.

title: Four skills-training areas
content: DBT skills training covers four broad areas: mindfulness, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness and distress tolerance.

title: Standard comprehensive outpatient DBT components
content: The standard outpatient DBT model described by ABCT includes weekly individual therapy, weekly skills training, as-needed between-session consultation and a weekly therapist consultation team. A programme missing components should be described as an adaptation rather than automatically called comprehensive DBT.

title: Individual therapy and target events
content: In the standard outpatient model described by ABCT, individual therapy addresses a high-priority event from the prior week, examines factors leading up to and following it, and identifies/practises alternative responses.

title: Skills generalization between sessions
content: Between-session consultation may help clients apply DBT skills outside the therapy hour. Availability and rules for contact depend on the programme and should be explained by the treating team.

title: Therapist consultation team
content: A therapist consultation team is a component of standard comprehensive outpatient DBT and provides clinicians with support and helps maintain adherence to DBT principles.

title: Comprehensive DBT versus adapted skills training
content: A service offering only some DBT components should not automatically be described as comprehensive DBT. Label the actual programme format clearly; evidence for partial-component programmes should not be assumed equivalent to comprehensive DBT.

title: Validation
content: Validation is consistent with DBT's acceptance side and is mentioned in NICE crisis-management guidance for people with borderline personality disorder. In the NICE context, clinicians should use empathic open questioning and avoid minimising the person's stated reasons for distress.

title: DBT applications beyond BPD
content: DBT has been adapted for other clinical problems, but evidence and programme formats differ by population and condition. Do not assume evidence for DBT in borderline personality disorder establishes equal effectiveness for every adapted use.

title: Outcome and duration expectations
content: Do not promise symptom resolution by a fixed date. ABCT notes that studies of DBT for BPD included treatment periods of a year or less, but that this does not mean everyone will be symptom-free at one year; duration varies by needs and context.

title: Medication boundary
content: The Copilot must not advise a client to start, stop or change medication. Medication decisions are outside the scope of a DBT skills record and must remain with an authorized prescriber and local clinical policy.

title: Suicide/self-harm risk boundary
content: DBT was originally developed for chronically suicidal individuals, and NICE provides separate risk and crisis-management recommendations for borderline personality disorder. A knowledge record cannot independently assess risk or replace a clinician's approved crisis pathway.

title: Crisis plan
